narrative:
The model determined that you have a 96% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and only accepts students with a strong likelihood of passing, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences. Placing in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3—compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students—strongly signaled to the model that you would struggle with the bar exam. These academic performance indicators outweighed everything else and pushed the prediction heavily toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 27 was the third most important factor. This is well below the average of 37 among accepted students and further increased the model’s confidence that you would not pass on the first try.

Although your middle family income, female gender, Asian background, plan to attend full-time, and 2.5 undergraduate GPA were considered, they had far less impact on the outcome than your class rankings and LSAT performance.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and test scores in a future application would likely change the model’s prediction and open the door to admission.
